title: Composition
summary: Assemble behavior by holding objects; inherit only when the type truly is-a subtype.

parts.rule: Composition builds behavior by giving an object collaborators and delegating work to them. Inheritance defines a subtype relationship: every child must be safe wherever the parent is accepted. Use composition for reuse and variation; reserve inheritance for a small, stable is-a relationship whose contract the child can fully honor.
parts.why: A subclass is coupled to protected state, lifecycle hooks, and assumptions in its base class. Reusing one method may accidentally inherit ten behaviors. A composed collaborator has an explicit interface, can be replaced in a test, and can often be reused around several implementations. The extra delegation is usually cheaper than a brittle hierarchy.
parts.example: UserRepo exposes find(id). SqlUserRepo takes about 20 ms to load a row. You want repeated reads near 1 ms. Inheriting CachedUserRepo from SqlUserRepo looks convenient, but it binds caching to SQL and may bypass cache behavior when a base method calls an internal query hook. Instead, CachedUserRepo holds two collaborators: an inner UserRepo and a Cache. find(42) checks key user:42; on a miss it calls inner.find(42), stores the result for 60 seconds, and returns it. The same wrapper can hold SqlUserRepo today and HttpUserRepo later. A unit test injects FakeUserRepo and verifies that two find(42) calls reach the fake only once. Composition also makes invalidation explicit through a delete or save path rather than hiding it in inherited overrides. Inheritance is appropriate when substitution is real: CsvReport and PdfReport may both implement Report, but neither needs to inherit implementation from the other. The classic warning is Square extending mutable Rectangle. If a caller sets width=4 and height=2, it expects area 8; a Square override that forces both sides to 2 breaks that parent contract. Shared helper code is not enough to make Square a Rectangle subtype.
parts.use: Default to composition for policies, storage clients, clocks, caches, and other behavior that may vary or need a fake in tests. Inject the narrow interface the object needs. Choose inheritance only after stating the parent contract and showing that the child preserves it without disabling or surprising inherited operations.
parts.refuse: Do not create a subclass merely to access helpers; extract a helper or collaborator. A child that overrides methods to throw, does nothing for half the API, or changes core postconditions is not substitutable. Composition can also be overdone: do not split a cohesive five-line calculation across a web of one-method objects without a real variation point.

body:
Rule. Composition builds behavior by giving an object collaborators and delegating work to them. Inheritance defines a subtype relationship: every child must be safe wherever the parent is accepted. Use composition for reuse and variation; reserve inheritance for a small, stable is-a relationship whose contract the child can fully honor.

Why it matters. A subclass is coupled to protected state, lifecycle hooks, and assumptions in its base class. Reusing one method may accidentally inherit ten behaviors. A composed collaborator has an explicit interface, can be replaced in a test, and can often be reused around several implementations. The extra delegation is usually cheaper than a brittle hierarchy.

Worked example. UserRepo exposes find(id). SqlUserRepo takes about 20 ms to load a row. You want repeated reads near 1 ms. Inheriting CachedUserRepo from SqlUserRepo looks convenient, but it binds caching to SQL and may bypass cache behavior when a base method calls an internal query hook. Instead, CachedUserRepo holds two collaborators: an inner UserRepo and a Cache. find(42) checks key user:42; on a miss it calls inner.find(42), stores the result for 60 seconds, and returns it. The same wrapper can hold SqlUserRepo today and HttpUserRepo later. A unit test injects FakeUserRepo and verifies that two find(42) calls reach the fake only once. Composition also makes invalidation explicit through a delete or save path rather than hiding it in inherited overrides. Inheritance is appropriate when substitution is real: CsvReport and PdfReport may both implement Report, but neither needs to inherit implementation from the other. The classic warning is Square extending mutable Rectangle. If a caller sets width=4 and height=2, it expects area 8; a Square override that forces both sides to 2 breaks that parent contract. Shared helper code is not enough to make Square a Rectangle subtype.

[[diagram:compose]]

When to use. Default to composition for policies, storage clients, clocks, caches, and other behavior that may vary or need a fake in tests. Inject the narrow interface the object needs. Choose inheritance only after stating the parent contract and showing that the child preserves it without disabling or surprising inherited operations.

When to refuse. Do not create a subclass merely to access helpers; extract a helper or collaborator. A child that overrides methods to throw, does nothing for half the API, or changes core postconditions is not substitutable. Composition can also be overdone: do not split a cohesive five-line calculation across a web of one-method objects without a real variation point.
